passages.original: Resurrectio Christi est redemptio corporis nostri. Vel exspectamus glorificationem in resurrectionem futuram corporis nostri : ut corruptum hoc induatur incorruptione. Hoc eopilulum obscurum est, inquit Augustinus, quia non satis apparet quam nunc vocet creaturam. Dicitur autem secundum catholicam disciplinam creatura, quidquid fecit et condidit Deus Pater, per unigenitum Filium suum, in unitate Spiritus sancti. Ergo non solum corpora, sed et animæ nostra, id cst spiritus nomine cicaturæ continentur. Sic autem dictum est, ipsa creatura liberabitur a servitute corruptionio in libertatem gloriæ filiorum Dei : quasi nos non simus creatura, sed filii Dei, in quorum gleriæ libertatem liberabitur a servitute creatum.
passages.english: The resurrection of Christ is the redemption of our body. Or: we await glorification in the future resurrection of our body, so that this corruptible thing may put on incorruption. "This little chapter is obscure," says Augustine, "because it is not clear enough what he here calls 'creation'." Now according to catholic teaching, whatever God the Father made and established through his only-begotten Son, in the unity of the Holy Spirit, is called creation. Therefore not only our bodies but also our souls, that is, our spirits, are contained under the name of creation. Yet it was said thus, "creation itself will be set free from the bondage of corruption into the liberty of the glory of the children of God," as if we were not creation but children of God, into the liberty of whose glory the created [thing] will be set free from bondage.
passages.notes: "eopilulum" read as "capitulum" (cf. the text after the passage); "cicaturæ" as "creaturae"; "corruptionio" as "corruptionis"; "gleriæ" as "gloriae"; "creatum" may be a corruption of "creatura".

passages.original: Hoc est, gratia Dei me vivificavit, et refecit, et post hæc cum Deigratia laboravi, etinme vacua non fuit.Et quia dixerat: Abundantius illis omnibus laboravi, ne sibi aliquid videretur ascribere, continuo subjunxit : Non ego autem, sed gratia Dei mecum : quia Deus in nobis operatur, et ipse nos ut laboremus inspirat, et ipse adjuvat laborantes, ipse opus bonum consummat : quia ex ipso, et per ipsum, et in ipso sunt omnia. Sicut et alibi dicit: Qui coepit in vobis opus bonum, ipse perficiet usque in diem Christi Jesu. Et ipse dicit: Sine me nihil potestis facere. Nam et beatus Hieronymus in Apologetico ad Pammachium, sic ponit testimonium istud : Non autem ego, sed gratia Dei, quae in me est. Sive enim ego, sive illi, sic prædicavimus, et sic credidistis. Si autem Christus prædicatur quod surrexit a mortuis, quomodo dicunt quidam in vobis, quoniam resurrectio mortuorum non est ? Si autem resurrectio mortuorum non est, neque Christus resurrexit.
passages.english: That is, the grace of God gave me life and restored me, and after this I laboured with the grace of God, and in me it was not in vain. And because he had said, "I laboured more abundantly than all of them," so that he might not seem to ascribe anything to himself, he at once added: "Yet not I, but the grace of God with me"; for God works in us, and he himself inspires us to labour, and he himself helps those who labour, he himself brings the good work to completion, because from him and through him and in him are all things. As he also says elsewhere: "He who began a good work in you will himself complete it until the day of Christ Jesus." And he himself says: "Without me you can do nothing." For blessed Jerome too, in the Apology to Pammachius, gives this testimony thus: "Yet not I, but the grace of God which is in me." "For whether I or they, so we have preached, and so you have believed. But if Christ is preached, that he rose from the dead, how do some among you say that there is no resurrection of the dead? But if there is no resurrection of the dead, neither has Christ risen."

passages.original: Quid tam Dei opus, quam Scripturas legere, in ecclesia prædicare, sacerdotium capere, ante altare Domini minisI rare. Sed hæc, nisi aliquis omni diligentia cuslodierit cor suum, de cupiditate laudis oriuntur. Videas plerosque (quod etiam Tullius ait) libros suos do contemnenda gloria inscribere, et causa gloriæ proprii nominis titulos prænotare. Interpretantur Scripturas saepe , et quae digna lectione sunt scribimus, et nisi causa Christi fiant, sed memoriæ in posteros, et famae in populos, tutus labor irrilus fiet : et erimus quasi tympanum sonans, et cymbalum concrepans.
passages.english: What is so much God's work as to read the Scriptures, to preach in the church, to take up the priesthood, to minister before the altar of the Lord? But these things, unless one guards his heart with all diligence, arise from the desire for praise. You may see many (as Tullius also says) inscribe on their books [the title] "On despising glory", and for the sake of glory set the titles of their own name at the head. We often interpret the Scriptures and write things worthy of reading, and unless they are done for Christ's sake, but [are done] for remembrance among posterity and for fame among the peoples, all the labour will become void, and we shall be like a sounding drum and a clanging cymbal.
passages.notes: "tutus labor irrilus" read as "totus labor irritus". "Interpretantur" (they interpret) seems to conflict with "scribimus"; rendered as first person. The "nisi... sed" construction is awkward; sense given.

passages.original: In Deo autem quia conditio temporis vacat: non enim potest recte videri Deus in tempore generasse Filium, per quem condidit tempora : consequens est ut non solum sit imago ejus, quia de illo est, et similitudo, quia imago; sed etiam æqualitas tanta, ut nec temporis quidem intervallum impedimentum sit. Item aliter. Cur imago similitudinem habet in picturis, homines nolunt esse dissimiles ? et Arius dissimilem contendit, et vult ut pater dissimilem generet sui. Primogenitus omnis creaturæ. Omnis rationabilis crea. turæ secundum carnem primus effectus, primogenitus, inquit, non primo creatus, ut et genitus pro natura, et primus pro perpetuitate credatur : vel certo primogenitus ex mortuis.
passages.english: But in God, since the condition of time is absent (for God cannot rightly be thought to have begotten in time the Son through whom he founded the times), it follows that there is not only his image, because he is from him, and likeness, because [he is] image, but also an equality so great that not even an interval of time is an impediment. Likewise, another way. Why does an image have likeness in paintings, [and] people do not want [them] to be unlike? Yet Arius contends that [the Son] is unlike, and wants the Father to beget one unlike himself. "The firstborn of every creature." Made first of every rational creature according to the flesh: "firstborn," he says, not "first created," so that he may be believed both "born" with respect to nature and "first" with respect to perpetuity; or certainly "firstborn from the dead."
passages.notes: The question about paintings is obscure in the Latin as printed ("Cur imago similitudinem habet in picturis, homines nolunt esse dissimiles?"); the sense seems to be that even human painters want an image to resemble its original. "certo" read as "certe" (certainly).

passages.original: Quod amem dicit, pro omnibus illum gustasse mortem, quidam doctores ita absoluteintelligunt, ut dicatur, pro omnibus pro quibus gustavit, id est pro electis, ad vitam aeternam prædestinatis. At vero quidam ita generaliter accipiunt, ut dicatur, pro omnibus mortuus est; licet omnes non salventur. Et quid si omnes non credunt? illc tamen quod suum erat, fecit. Unde beatus Prosper banc ponit similitudinem : Est quilibet medicorum peritissimus, qui veniens in civitatem populosam, uhi multi infirmi habentur, temperat potionem contra omnia genera infirmitatum, et convo- cat omnes, dicens : Venite, omnes populi, qui variis infirmitatibus laboratis, et bibite ex hac potione, quam causa salutis vestrae praeparavi: spendeo vobis cum obtestatione quod si quis biberit ex ea medelam Statim consequi merebitur.
passages.english: As for his saying that he tasted death for all, some teachers understand it so absolutely that it is said [to mean]: for all for whom he tasted [it], that is, for the elect, predestined to eternal life. But some take it so generally that it is said: he died for all, although not all are saved. And what if not all believe? He nevertheless did what was his [to do]. Hence blessed Prosper offers this comparison: There is some most skilful physician who, coming into a populous city where there are many sick, mixes a potion against all kinds of illness and calls everyone together, saying: "Come, all you people who suffer from various illnesses, and drink of this potion which I have prepared for the sake of your health; I promise you solemnly that if anyone drinks of it, he will deserve to obtain healing at once."
passages.notes: "Quod amem" read as "Quod autem"; "absoluteintelligunt" as "absolute intelligunt" — possibly "absolute" is an error for a restrictive sense; "spendeo" as "spondeo".

passages.original: et benedixerit ei, decimasque prædæ atque victoriae ab eo acceperit, sicut sacerdos Excelsi et summi Dei , non falsoruin deorum et idolorum : qui fuit etiam rex Salem. Salem autem, sicut beatus Hieronymus dicit, non est putanda Hierusalem, ut Josephus historiographus nostrorumque plurimi arbitrantur: sed oppidum est juxta Scythopolim, quod usque hodie appellatur Salcm sive Salim : de quo, teste beato Hieronymo, in Evan- gelio tegitur : Erat ( inquit Joannes) baptizans in Ennon ju-xta Salim, quia aquae multæ erant illic. Idcirco autem flt ista varietas nominum, quia Hebræis multis in locis per consonantes solummodo scribunt subtractis vocalibus, atque ita secundum arbitrium legentis pronuntiatur non uno semper eodemque modo.
passages.english: and blessed him, and received from him the tithes of the spoil and victory, as priest of the Most High and supreme God, not of false gods and idols; who was also king of Salem. Salem, however, as blessed Jerome says, is not to be thought to be Jerusalem, as Josephus the historian and very many of our [writers] suppose, but is a town near Scythopolis which to this day is called Salem or Salim; of which, on the testimony of blessed Jerome, one reads in the Gospel: "John," it says, "was baptizing in Aenon near Salim, because there was much water there." This variety of names arises because the Hebrews in many places write only with consonants, the vowels omitted, and so it is pronounced according to the judgement of the reader, not always in one and the same way.

passages.original: Quod autem dicit sæcula perfecta esse verbo Dei, per saecula debemus intelligere omnia quae facta sunt in tempora sive sæcula verbo Dei Patris, juxta quod Joannes dixit: Omnia per ipsum facta sunt. Sæcula vero, ut Ovidius Naso dicit, dicuntur a sequendo, eo quod sese sequantur atque revolvantur, teste Varrone. Sæcula autem ex eo dici possunt, ex quo varietas coepit esse temporis. Fide plurimam hostiam Abel quam Cain obtulit Deo per quam testimonium consecutus est esse justus, testimonium perhibente Deo muneribus ejus : et per illam defunctus adhuc loquitur.
passages.english: As for his saying that the ages were perfected by the word of God, by "ages" we ought to understand all things that were made in times or ages by the Word of God the Father, according to what John said: "All things were made through him." Now "ages" (saecula), as Ovid Naso says, are so called from "following" (sequendo), because they follow one another and revolve, as Varro attests. And ages can be said [to exist] from the moment when the variation of time began. "By faith Abel offered to God a greater sacrifice than Cain, through which he obtained testimony that he was righteous, God bearing testimony to his gifts; and through it, though dead, he still speaks."
passages.notes: The derivation of saeculum from sequor is attributed here to Ovid and Varro; the attribution to Ovid is doubtful. "Fide plurimam hostiam" = Heb. 11:4 ("plurimam" meaning "greater", as the following context explains).
